Password hash sync
Password hash sync is the simplest method to enable authentication for on-premises Active
Directory idx_56b87193 objects in the cloud. In this method, password idx_40e7c0b0 hashes are synchronized to Microsoft
Entra ID. The users can use the same usernames and passwords for all on-premises and cloud
applications. It idx_0b3398e8 offers the following key advantages:
Requires the least amount of administrative effort in terms of deployment,

Advanced identity protection features like leaked credential reports are available only
with this method.
Provides business continuity. If your on-premises Active Directory infrastructure is not
available, the users will still be able to authenticate.
Password hash sync can be used as a fallback mechanism for the other two
authentication methods. If you have certain business requirements that are not met by
password hash sync, you can use one of the other two methods and use password hash
idx_e44670ab sync as a fallback method to continue providing authentication services to your end
users in case your on-premises infrastructure is unavailable.
It also enables leaked credentials detection for hybrid accounts. Microsoft works with
security researchers and law enforcement to find username/password pairs that are
publicly available. If such accounts are found, Microsoft Entra flags them as high risk.
The on-premises idx_2f8c00f1 Active Directory stores user passwords as an MD4 hash idx_829fe2b1 value of the original
password. This is the result of a hashing algorithm, which is a one-way mathematical function.
There is no way that a hashed value can be reversed to obtain the original password.
Microsoft Entra Connect sync extracts the password hash from Active Directory and applies
additional security to the hashed password before synchronizing it with Microsoft Entra ID.
The passwords are synchronized every two minutes, and this interval cannot be modified.
On the first run, all passwords of in-scope users are synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID. You
can use staged rollout to test user groups with capabilities like MFA, Conditional Access,

The plain-text passwords are never exposed to the password hash synchronization

The passwords are never stored in SQL. They are only processed in memory and then

Microsoft Entra Domain Services
In the last few years, we have seen a major shift to cloud services. However, many
organizations still have a significant portion of their infrastructure on premises. While
Microsoft Entra provides identity and access management services in the cloud, some
organizations idx_e34c3c97 still rely on Active Directory services like domain join, group policy, and
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)/ Kerberos authentication. Microsoft Entra
Domain Services provides managed domain idx_da42f87c services in the cloud to organizations with such
requirements. It enables organizations to use familiar Active Directory features without
deploying, managing, or patching domain controllers. This is especially useful for scenarios
where an organization wants to reduce its on-premises footprint, but a hybrid identity solution
is necessary to support both on-premises and cloud resources. Using this solution,
organizations can migrate legacy, directory-dependent applications to the cloud with minimal
redevelopment. This chapter will cover:

Common deployment scenarios
Deploying Microsoft Entra Domain Services

Cloud-based directory services
As organizations increasingly transition their workloads to the cloud, the need for legacy
support remains, particularly for applications and resources that depend on directory services
like domain join, LDAP, Kerberos authentication, and group policy. Microsoft offers two ways
that provide idx_6b04e71e traditional Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) in the cloud.

Self-managed domain
A self-managed domain can be idx_2c69a4d5 created using resources like Virtual Machines (VMs),
Windows idx_3aa531bf Server, and AD DS. This is like installing and maintaining a traditional AD DS
environment in the cloud. Instead of physical servers, it is installed on VMs in the cloud. The
organization is responsible for managing, patching, and idx_a100505a securing the Domain Controllers
(DCs) and related infrastructure. Common deployment models for using a self-managed AD
DS environment include:
Standalone cloud-only AD DS: This is a completely independent AD DS environment
and does not integrate with an on-premises AD DS environment. This is useful for
organizations that would like to lift and shift their on-premises AD DS infrastructure to
the cloud.
Extend on-premises domain to Azure: In this approach, the on-premises Active
Directory Domain Services (AD DS) domain is extended into Azure by establishing
connectivity between an Azure virtual network and the on-premises network through
either a VPN or an ExpressRoute connection. Azure virtual machines are then joined to

this virtual network, enabling them to participate in and authenticate against the on-
premises AD DS environment. Azure VMs can also be promoted as additional DCs that
replicate over the VPN or ExpressRoute connection.
While this may be a quick and viable option for some organizations, they still retain the
overhead and management of the servers running the domain controllers. A managed domain
solves this problem as explained in the next section.
Overview of Microsoft Entra Domain Services
Microsoft Entra Domain Services offers a seamless way to extend Active Directory
capabilities to the cloud idx_f4d9e4f6 without the operational overhead of deploying, managing, or patching
VMs. By integrating with Microsoft Entra ID, it enables organizations to create a hybrid
identity infrastructure that supports both legacy and cloud-native applications, fostering
modernization and flexibility. Domain Services offers a smaller subset of features as compared
to self-managed domain, thereby reducing complexity. For example, there are no AD forests,
domain sites, or replication links to manage.
With this managed service, businesses can migrate directory-dependent workloads to the
cloud more efficiently, minimizing redevelopment and ensuring continuity for critical systems.
Entra Domain Services also helps improve security posture by leveraging cloud-based updates
and monitoring, reducing the risks associated with on-premises infrastructure. It is ideal for
organizations looking to reduce their on-premises footprint while maintaining compatibility
with established authentication and policy management tools. As enterprises embrace cloud-

Basic concepts
Before we idx_d6f1caad proceed with creating a managed domain, let's understand some important
concepts as there are some differences in how Domain Services behaves in comparison to an
on-premises AD DS environment.
Replica sets
When a managed domain is provisioned, Azure automatically deploys two Windows DCs
within the idx_0d333c15 selected Azure region. This deployment, referred to as a replica set, provides
redundancy and high availability for the managed domain. A key advantage of using a
managed domain is that organizations are relieved of the responsibility for maintaining these
domain controllers, as Azure fully manages them as part of the service. This management
includes built-in features such as automated backups and encryption of data at rest, ensuring
both operational resilience and security compliance.
Managed domains can be expanded to include more than one replica set per Microsoft Entra
tenant. Replica sets can be added to any peered virtual network in any Azure region. This
provides geographical disaster recovery in case an Azure region becomes unavailable. All
replica sets share the same namespace and configuration and contain the same data. Any
changes, such as configuration, user identity, groups, or Group Policy objects are applied to all
replica sets using AD DS replication.
Each replica set is created in a virtual network that must be peered with every other virtual
network containing a replica set. A single virtual network can host multiple replica sets if each
one resides in a different subnet. You can create up to five replica sets per managed domain.
Forests and trusts
Forest is a logical idx_a6f4144e unit in Active Directory that can contain one or more domains. User objects,
groups, and devices are stored in domains. Domains also provide authentication services. In
Domain Services, a forest can contain only one domain.
A forest trust can be created with another domain to allow users access to resources.
Depending on requirements, the following types of trusts can be created:
Two-way: Users in both domains can access each other's resources. •

One-way outgoing: Users in the on-premises domain access resources in the managed
domain but users in the managed domain cannot access resources in the on-premises
domain.
One-way incoming: Users in the managed domain can access resources in the on-
premises idx_f86e55c3 domain but users in the on-premises domain cannot access resources in the
managed domain.
Synchronization
An automatic one-way synchronization is configured from Microsoft Entra ID to a managed

managed domain, but the resources created in the managed domain are not synchronized to
Microsoft Entra ID. Applications and services in the Azure environment connected to the
managed domain can take advantage of features like domain join, group policy, LDAP, and
Kerberos.
If organizations have a hybrid environment with on-premises AD that is connected to
Microsoft Entra ID using Microsoft Entra Connect, resources from on-premises AD are
synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID and from there they are automatically synchronized to the
managed domain. The following figure shows this:

objects to be synchronized. After the initial synchronization is complete, changes made in
Microsoft Entra ID are automatically synchronized to Domain Services.
It is possible to scope user synchronization to only the users that originated in the cloud. This
way users from the on-premises AD DS environment will not be synchronized to the managed
domain.

A managed domain is a DNS namespace and directory. The DCs that contain all resources like
users idx_896e061f and groups are part of the managed service and users cannot sign in to these DCs. A VM

While creating a managed domain, you will be asked to specify a DNS domain name. There

Built-in domain name: By default, the managed domain is assigned a name with
the .onmicrosoft.com suffix. This default naming convention is not recommended

Because Microsoft retains ownership of the .onmicrosoft.com namespace,

connections using the default domain name.
Custom domain names: It is recommended to use a custom domain that the
organization owns and is routable.
Non-routable domain suffixes: It is not recommended to use a non-routable domain
name such as litware.local. Because these domains are not routable, they can cause
issues with DNS resolution.
The following DNS name restrictions apply:
Managed domain names cannot contain a prefix that is longer than 15 characters.
The name should be unique in your virtual network. The following scenarios could

If you have an AD domain with the same DNS domain name on the Azure virtual

If the virtual network on which you plan to enable the managed domain is

If you have an existing Azure cloud service with the same name on the virtual

A trust relationship idx_0d687870 can be created between a managed domain and an idx_2ec8223e on-premises AD DS
environment. This trust enables users, applications, and devices from a managed domain to
authenticate against an on-premises domain and vice versa. A forest trust helps users access
resources in environments where password hashes cannot be synchronized or in passwordless
scenarios such as smart cards. It also enables access in hybrid environments that require access
to on-premises environments.
To enable forest trust, the following prerequisites must be met:
An active Azure subscription with a Microsoft Entra tenant associated. The Entra
tenant idx_a6c272a1 could be cloud-only or synchronized with an on-premises domain.
A Domain Services managed domain configured with a custom DNS and a valid SSL
certificate.
An on-premises domain that is reachable either via ExpressRoute or VPN connectivity.
The network must meet the following requirements:
Any firewall ports and DCs must allow traffic that is necessary to create a trust.
All DCs that need to have a trust with the managed domain must have these
ports open.
Use static private IP addresses.
Avoid overlapping IP address spaces to ensure successful communication
between Azure and on-premises.
Domain Services must have its own subnet.
Peered virtual networks should not be transitive.
Ensure continuous connectivity and DNS name resolution between Azure and
on-premises.
An account with Application Administrator and Groups Administrator role
assigned.
A Domain Administrator account for the on-premises domain.

The following idx_1702dc72 section explains some of the key security settings that must be enabled to secure

Securing managed domain
Microsoft Entra Domain Services allows the use of NTLM v1 and TLS v1 by default. These
ciphers idx_e130d42b may be required for some legacy applications to run, but they are considered insecure
and weak and must be disabled if there are no applications that need them. Microsoft is
deprecating the use of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. TLS 1.2 and later versions offer improved security
features such as perfect forward secrecy and stronger cipher suites.
To manage security settings for the managed domain, follow the steps below:

Navigate to Entra ID | Domain services. In the right pane, click on the managed

applications that still use earlier versions of TLS.
NTLM v1 Authentication: If this mode is enabled, all NTLM v1 requests will fail.
Password synchronization from On-premises: If this setting is disabled, on-
premises user accounts will not be able to authenticate in the managed domain.
NTLM Password Synchronization: If this setting is disabled, synchronized user
idx_c80033f5 accounts will not be able to use NTLM authentication in the managed domain.
Kerberos RC4 Encryption: If this is disabled, all Kerberos requests that use RC4
encryption will fail.
Kerberos Armoring: Enabling this setting will provide a secure channel between
Kerberos client and the Kerberos Distribution Center (KDC).
LDAP Signing: Enabling this setting will require all LDAP clients to request
signing during bind time.
LDAP Channel Binding: Enabling this setting will require all LDAP clients to
provide channel binding information while communicating with the directory.

Carefully consider the NTLM and TLS requirements for your organization and configure them
appropriately to ensure that applications continue to work without compromising security.
Configuring Kerberos constrained delegation
Some applications need to access resources in the context of a different user. AD DS supports a
idx_d2874284 mechanism called Kerberos delegation that lets one account impersonate another account to
access resources. For idx_4f53fd6d example, a website can impersonate another user to access back-end
resources. Kerberos delegation is considered idx_52a84546 insecure because it does not restrict which
resources an impersonating account can access. In contrast, Kerberos Constrained
Delegation (KCD) allows administrators to explicitly define the resources that can be accessed
on behalf of another user. Configuring KCD requires domain administrator privileges to enable
a domain account for a specific service, and the delegated account is limited to operating
within a single domain. A managed domain does not give Domain Administrator privileges, so
account-based KCD cannot be used. Domain Services managed domains use a more secure
resource-based KCD, available in Windows Server 2012 and later. This capability enables
administrators to configure constrained delegation for their services. Using resource-based
KCD, back-end service administrators can explicitly allow or deny specific front-end services
from performing delegation, thereby providing finer grained control over authentication flows.

The following idx_3d5cc6b8 are some key concepts of the principles of least privilege:
Access to only the required resources: This is the foundation of the principle of least
privilege. Users are given access to resources only if they have a genuine need to access
those resources to fulfill their job duties. This prevents unauthorized data access and
limits the impact of a security breach. Lifecycle workflows is a feature in identity
governance that helps organizations automate lifecycle processes.
Role-based Access Control (RBAC): Access is based on the role and job functions of
the user. Each role has the minimum permissions assigned that are necessary to fulfill
job requirements. Microsoft Entra RBAC manages access to Microsoft Entra resources.
Just-In-Time access: Users are granted access to resources only for the duration for
which they are needed and revoked when they are no longer required. This minimizes
idx_11d7bb38 the timeframe during which attackers could potentially exploit elevated privileges.
Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management is a solution that helps manage,
control, and monitor just-in-time access.
Regular audit and review: Organizations must perform periodic reviews of user
access to ensure that they still require the permissions that they have. This helps
ensure that there is no permission creep. Access reviews is a feature in Microsoft Entra
ID Governance that helps organizations automate access reviews.
Default deny: The principle of least privilege works on default deny. This means that,
by default, users are denied access, and access is explicitly granted only for approved
purposes.
By following these principles, organizations can reduce risk and ensure alignment with
business needs.
Entitlement management

sites, Teams channels, and applications. New employees may not initially know which
resources are idx_8d0eadf3 necessary. After joining, they often need time to determine what access is
required and to identify the appropriate approvers for their access requests. This process can
delay the point at which the employee becomes fully productive. The situation can become
more complex when collaborating with other organizations, as it may be unclear who in the
external organization requires access to specific resources.

Understanding catalogs

Multi-stage reviews
Access reviews support up to three review stages. This enables multiple approvers to review
access to idx_fa931a08 resources before a decision is made. It helps organizations meet certification and
audit requirements, design more efficient reviews, and reduce the number of decisions each
reviewer is responsible for.
Multi-stage idx_218dc683 reviews help meet the following use cases:
Reach consensus across multiple reviewers: This might be useful when access to
highly critical resources is being reviewed or when there is a diverse set of reviewees,
and it is hard for a single reviewer to make the decision.
Get input on unreviewed decisions: If the first stage approvers are unable to decide,
second stage and third stage reviewers can help.
Reduce burden on later-stage reviewers: Reviews can be configured in such a way
that if a deny decision is made at an earlier stage, those users are not reviewed at the
later stages. This way the subsequent stage approvers see a filtered down list.
The options idx_b54086ae available while configuring multi-stage review are:
Reviewers: Group owners, selected users or groups, users themselves, or managers of
users can be configured as reviewers. For group owners, selected users or groups and
managers of users, fallback reviewers can be configured. These will be used if primary
reviewers do not exist.
Stage duration: This specifies the number of days within which reviewers at each
stage must respond to the review request.
Show previous stage(s) decision to later stage reviewers: You can choose to reveal or
hide the decision taken by earlier stage reviewers by selecting or deselecting this box.
Review recurrence: You can specify if the access review is one time or recurring. The
available options are One time, Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly, Semi-annually, and
Annually. If you choose a recurring review, you can specify start date and end options
like Never, End on specific date, or End after number of occurrences.
Reviewees going to next stage: Lastly, you can choose to send all or only a subset of
reviewees to the next stage. The available options are All, Approved reviewees,
Denied reviewees, Not reviewed reviewees, and Reviewees marked as "Don't
know".

Workflows
Lifecycle workflows play a critical role in modern identity and access management by
streamlining and automating the processes associated with a user's journey within an
organization. From the moment a new employee joins (the joiner), through internal changes
such as promotions or department transfers (the mover), to when they leave the company (the
leaver), each stage demands precise updates to access rights and group memberships to
maintain both productivity and security. Manual management of these transitions is not only
time-consuming but also prone to errors, which can lead to unauthorized access or overlooked
permissions, posing significant security risks.
By leveraging lifecycle workflows, organizations can ensure that user accounts are provisioned,
updated, and deprovisioned automatically and consistently. This automation supports
compliance with regulatory requirements by providing clear audit trails of access changes and
minimizing the risk of data breaches due to lingering or excessive permissions. Additionally,
lifecycle workflows improve operational efficiency by reducing the administrative burden on IT
teams, allowing them to focus on more strategic initiatives. The use of predefined templates
and integration with HR tools further accelerates deployment and ensures that the workflows
reflect organizational policies and best practices.

Introduction to Microsoft Entra Lifecycle Workflows
Lifecycle Workflows (LCW) is a feature in Microsoft Entra ID Governance that enables
organizations idx_0bb3f8c4 to manage users by automating the lifecycle processes of joiner, mover, and
leaver. Workflows contain processes that run automatically for users as they move through the
identity lifecycle.
Organizations idx_80723632 that want to modernize their identity lifecycle management process need to
ensure that users have the correct access to the correct resources, groups, and applications on
the day they join the organization. They also must ensure that access is revoked in a timely
manner for users who have left the organization. It is also important that the process of
provisioning and revoking access is not overly complicated and time-consuming for
administrators. Administrators should also be able to troubleshoot problems and have access
to logs that help with troubleshooting, audit, and compliance.
There are several reasons why an organization would like to use lifecycle workflows. Some of

Extend the HR-driven provisioning process with other workflows to simplify and

location.

Manage the identity and access management lifecycle at scale.
Automate manual tasks.
Use logic apps to extend the capability for more complex scenarios.
The capabilities in lifecycle workflows help remove dependencies and increase efficiency in

LCW as a Zero Trust control
The Zero Trust security model operates on three foundational principles: verify explicitly, use
least-privilege access, and assume breach. In environments where identity has replaced the
network idx_d4a68714 perimeter as the primary control plane, these principles demand that every user
account be continuously validated, scoped to the minimum necessary permissions, and treated
as a potential vector for compromise.
LCW provides the automation framework that translates these Zero Trust principles into
operational reality. By orchestrating identity actions across the joiner-mover-leaver cycle,
LCW ensures that access is granted, adjusted, and revoked in a timely, policy-driven manner,

52662.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
52662.heading: Chapter 7 228
52662.content:
eliminating the manual gaps that attackers exploit.
Every active identity in a directory represents a potential entry point for an attacker. The
identity attack surface grows not only with the number of accounts, but also with the
privileges those accounts hold and the duration for which those privileges persist. Lifecycle
workflows reduce this surface across all three dimensions:
Account proliferation control: Joiner workflows ensure that accounts are created
through governed, template-driven processes with predefined group memberships,
•

52663.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
52663.heading: Chapter 7 230
52663.content:
Chapter 7 230
license assignments, and access packages. This prevents the ad hoc account creation
that leads to ungoverned identities.
Privilege scoping: Mover workflows automatically adjust access when users change
roles, departments, or locations. Rather than accumulating permissions across job
changes, users receive only what their current role requires, enforcing the least-
privilege principle at every transition.
Timely deprovisioning: Leaver workflows disable accounts, revoke group
memberships, remove licenses, and schedule account deletion based on the
employeeLeaveDateTime attribute, ensuring that departing users cannot retain access
beyond their last day.
Together, these idx_0673be6f automated actions produce a continuously right-sized identity footprint.
Rather than relying on periodic manual reviews to discover and remediate over-provisioned or
stale accounts, LCW maintains hygiene as a continuous, event-driven process.
Let's explore how LCW acts as a Zero Trust control in each phase of the identity lifecycle.
Joiner phase
The joiner phase is where Zero Trust begins. New employees often wait days for access to the
tools they idx_d6e8927a need and when access finally arrives, it is frequently over-provisioned because
administrators grant broad permissions to avoid repeated requests.
LCW joiner workflows solve both problems simultaneously. By defining access packages tied to
specific roles and departments, the workflow grants exactly the permissions new employees
need, before their first day. This approach delivers immediate productivity while enforcing the
principle of least privilege from the moment the identity is created.
Pre-hire tasks can include generating a Temporary Access Pass, sending a welcome email with
onboarding instructions, and adding the user to their department's Microsoft Teams channels
and security groups. These tasks can be triggered automatically based on the
employeeHireDate attribute.
Mover phase
When users idx_b009163b change roles, they gradually accumulate permissions as their previous access is
seldom revoked. This privilege drift is one of the most persistent and insidious violations of the
least privilege principle. In organizations without mover automation, a user who moves from
finance to marketing may retain access to financial systems, sensitive reports, and
administrative tools that are no longer relevant to their role.
•
•
231 Microsoft Entra Lifecycle Workflows
Over time, these accumulated permissions create accounts with far more access than any
single role requires. These over-privileged accounts are prime targets for attackers because
compromising one account yields access to multiple organizational functions.
LCW mover idx_f7e2e0b9 workflows address privilege drift by automatically detecting attribute changes like

52664.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
52664.heading: Chapter 7 230
52664.content:
updates to department or job title and executing a defined sequence of access adjustments.
Previous group memberships are removed, new role-appropriate access packages are assigned,
and the transition is logged for audit purposes. This approach enforces the principle of least
privilege access.
Leaver phase
The leaver phase represents the highest risk moment in the identity lifecycle from a Zero Trust
perspective. A departing employee's account, if left active, becomes an unmonitored identity
with valid idx_eacce20d credentials and established permissions. These serve as gold mines for attackers as
they can compromise these accounts and launch multi-stage attacks that can compromise
hybrid cloud environments, perform lateral movement, exfiltrate data, steal credentials, and
deploy ransomware in the environment.
Hybrid environments introduce a particular challenge for deprovisioning. When an employee
departs, their identity typically exists in multiple locations such as on-premises AD, Entra ID,
connected SaaS applications, and potentially downstream systems provisioned through SCIM
or custom connectors.
In organizations that rely on manual or ticket-based deprovisioning, the delay between an
employee's departure and the revocation of their access across all systems can range from days
to weeks. During that interval, the risk profile is severe. Even if the cloud account is disabled,
an on-premises AD account may remain active, providing access to file shares, VPN gateways,
and domain-joined resources. Applications provisioned outside the core identity platform may
not receive deprovisioning signals, leaving orphaned access in downstream systems.
LCW leaver workflows transform deprovisioning from a reactive, ticket-based process into a
deterministic, policy-driven operation. Whether triggered by the employeeLeaveDateTime
attribute for planned departures or executed on demand for immediate terminations, the
workflow ensures consistent, complete, and auditable offboarding across configured identity
systems. This approach enforces the principles of assume breach and least privilege access.
Lifecycle workflows are not merely an operational convenience. They are a foundational Zero
Trust idx_d54bd4d7 control. In an environment where identity is the perimeter, the hygiene of the identity
directory directly determines the organization's security posture. LCW ensures that:
Every identity is created with the minimum necessary permissions (verify explicitly,
least privilege).
•

Every role change triggers an automatic rebalancing of access (least privilege,
continuous verification).
Every departure results in timely, complete deprovisioning (assume breach, attack
surface reduction).
By automating the joiner–mover–leaver cycle, organizations move from a model of periodic,
manual identity governance to one of continuous, policy-driven enforcement.

Existing application: Choose an existing application or a system or user-

Privileged identities are a critical component in modern security strategies, particularly for
organizations utilizing cloud and hybrid environments. These identities refer to accounts or
users that are granted elevated permissions, enabling them to perform sensitive operations,
such as managing user access, configuring systems, or administering critical resources.
Because these accounts hold the keys to an organization's most important assets, their
management must be robust, systematic, and auditable.
Effective management of privileged identities involves several best practices. Firstly, access
should be granted only when absolutely necessary, following the principle of least privilege.
This means limiting the scope and duration of elevated access, so that users only have the
necessary idx_216ef8f9 permissions for the task at hand and only for as long as needed. Microsoft Entra
Privileged Identity Management (PIM) facilitates this by providing just-in-time and time-
bound access, requiring approval workflows, and enforcing multi-factor authentication for role
activation. Additionally, regular access reviews and justification requests ensure that privileges
are not retained longer than required, reducing the risk of misuse or compromise.
By centralizing and automating the management of privileged identities, organizations can
significantly reduce their attack surface, maintain compliance with regulatory requirements,
and improve overall security posture.
This chapter will cover:
Introduction to privileged identities
Deploying Privileged Identity Management
Managing Privileged Identity Management
Auditing PIM
Introduction to privileged identities
Privileged identities are specialized accounts or users within an organization that have been
granted elevated permissions, allowing them to perform critical and sensitive operations that
go beyond idx_1a49506e what standard users can do. These identities are central to the administration of IT
systems, cloud services, and data resources because they have the authority to manage user
access, configure infrastructure, oversee system security, and even alter or delete vital data. In a
modern business environment the concept of privileged identities has become a cornerstone in
the defense against cyber threats and the assurance of regulatory compliance.
Service accounts used by applications to access databases or perform automated tasks may
also be considered privileged if they are granted broad access rights. Because these identities
hold the "keys to the kingdom," they are highly attractive targets for cyber attackers. If
compromised, a privileged account can be used to escalate attacks, exfiltrate sensitive data, or
disrupt business operations on a large scale.

52701.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
52701.heading: Chapter 7 260
52701.content:
Managing privileged identities effectively is critical. The management of privileged identities
involves several key strategies. First, access to privileged roles should be time-bound and just-
in-time. Instead of granting permanent elevated access, organizations should provide
privileged access only when it is needed and for a limited duration. Microsoft Entra
Privileged Identity Management (PIM) automates this process by allowing users to activate
privileged roles only after passing additional checks or approval workflows. These controls
ensure that access is not only temporary but also auditable, providing a clear record of who
accessed what resources and when.
In summary, privileged identities are essential but high-risk. Strong controls are essential to
protect critical systems and minimize an organization's attack surface.

to resources and oversee what they are doing with that access.

It provides just-in-time access to Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources
It provides time-bound access to resources
It can require approval to activate privileged roles
It can enforce MFA to activate privileged roles
It can ask for justification to activate the privileged role
Access reviews can be conducted to ensure users still need the roles
Notifications can be sent when privileged roles are activated
Audit history is maintained for internal or external audits

Plan PIM deployment
Planning a PIM deployment is a critical step for organizations aiming to enhance their security
posture and idx_986e0984 manage access to sensitive resources effectively. Without thorough planning,
organizations may face challenges in assigning the correct roles, ensuring compliance, and
maintaining visibility over privileged activities. A well-conceived deployment plan helps
identify which roles require PIM, ensures that all licensing requirements are met, and
establishes clear processes for approval and activation workflows. This preparation not only
minimizes the risk of unauthorized access but also streamlines the user experience for those
who legitimately need elevated privileges.
Furthermore, planning allows organizations to align PIM implementation with broader IT
governance and compliance objectives. By mapping out business needs, regulatory
requirements, and operational processes beforehand, organizations can configure PIM settings
—such as approval requirements, notification policies, and auditing mechanisms—in a way
that supports both security and productivity. It also provides an opportunity to educate
stakeholders about the new processes, reducing confusion and resistance during rollout. A
strategic approach to PIM deployment ensures that privileged access is granted only when
necessary, for the right duration, and under proper oversight, thereby reducing the attack
surface and supporting ongoing risk management efforts.
It is recommended idx_8d2e57bb to start with a pilot which will consist of a small set of test users to ensure
that PIM behaves as expected. Develop test cases to test all aspects of PIM, like PIM for Entra
roles, Azure roles, and groups. This should include members of a group, members of a role, IT
service owner, subscription or resource owner in Azure and owners of groups. This way you
can verify that all configuration is set up correctly and move to production with confidence.
Communication is critical for the success of PIM. Proactively communicate with users and
educate them on how their experience will change and how they can get support if required. It
is also important to have a rollback plan in place in case PIM fails to work as desired.

Group memberships often grant broad, high-impact access across Azure and Microsoft 365.
When idx_1bbc295f groups are assigned to privileged roles, any permanent membership becomes a standing

PIM supports Microsoft Entra Security groups or M365 groups.
